source_text: 🈖: right, so maybe there's a little "pager-like" mechanism, i.e., check top 10, then next 10 if nothing found, etc.?  Isn't this a little bit like "beam search"?
reply_text:
㊟ ("a little bit like beam search") Similar, with one important difference. Beam search keeps the top k candidates and throws the rest away for good, so it can miss the answer. A pager only postpones the rest: if nothing in the first ten works out, it turns to the next ten, so every move can still be reached eventually.

🈖 (the closest relatives) Your pager has standard names:
- **Progressive widening** is the search-tree version. A position starts with only its few most promising moves, and more are added as the search keeps visiting it, usually in proportion to a power of the visit count. It's the standard method for game trees with too many moves to list. Combined with an order from the policy network, it's exactly your pager: top 10 first, the next 10 once those have had their share of visits.
- **Staged move generation** in chess engines is the same idea for listing moves. Generate captures first, and generate quiet moves only if no capture has already settled things.

🈖 (why it fits here) Our cost is checking moves, not ranking them. With the pager, a new position costs about 10 checks rather than 532. Wrong guesses cost one check each: the network was trained only on legal moves, so most of its top choices should be legal. The rule for when to open the next page can be the standard one, opening it when the visit count passes the next threshold. That way the search widens where it keeps coming back, and stays narrow elsewhere.

㊭ (next) If P16's split confirms that listing moves is the main cost, I'll write the packet: our own search using progressive widening ordered by the network, checking legality only page by page. Its test: stage 1 wins as before, and on the 20 recorded wins the new search chooses the same moves as the full search. That's ahead of any overnight run.
